newsitem.title: MEXICO: FORECAST - Serfin seen with big 1996 loss.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Serfin seen with big 1996 loss.

text.p: Grupo Financiero Serfin, owner of Mexico's third largest bank, will probably report big losses in 1996 as it cleans up its grimy past-due loan portfolio to prepare for a partial sale to a foreign partner, analysts said.

According to Serfin spokesman Roberto Aguirre, the bank is not planning to report its results until late February, and in the meantime it is continuing talks with two potential partners -- London-based HSBC Holdings Plc and a U.S. bank that he declined to name.
He said 19.9 percent of the banking group is up for sale, denying market rumors that the stake could be increased.
Financial analysts said the release of the results could coincide with the announcement of the sale, but Aguirre denied there was any intention to coordinate the two items of news.

Among analysts, the heaviest-backed candidate is HSBC. Aguirre said its board and Serfin's board were currently mulling each other's proposals, but he also mentioned the other U.S. suitor, which several analysts said they had not heard about. He said Serfin hoped for a sale "as soon as possible."

In order to spruce up the bank for the potential union, analysts said Serfin is likely to have reserved heavily against past-due loans and written off or reclassified as past-due loans that had hitherto been considered current.
Serfin has a chunk of unpaid mortgage and toll road loans outstanding that it has not yet recognized as past due.
"They're going to post a large loss," said Carlos Gomez, bank analyst at Paribas in New York.
"The reason is not just that they are going to have to reclassify their loans. They are very close to finishing negotiations with HSBC...and HSBC will naturally demand to see a clear picture.
"Anything that they have not classified (as past-due) in the past will probably be written off," he speculated.
He added that he expected most provisioning to be recognized on the income statement, rather than as a charge to equity, saying losses could be in the "billions of pesos."
Over the year, said Jose Garcia-Cantera, Latin American bank analyst at Salomon Brothers, Serfin's loss was bound to be big, "because of all the provisions they have made and very weak margins."

Mexican banks have mostly revealed a higher-than-expected jump in past-due loans under new U.S. GAAP accounting standards that took effect Jan. 1. If Serfin also reported loans under U.S. GAAP, they would not be expected to buck that trend.
Where the group is expected to take a worse hit than its two larger counterparts is on interest margins.
Petru Vaduva, Latin American bank analyst at ING Barings, said the bank's interest margins are almost half those of some of its stronger rivals, such as Banorte.
"That's a major blow to your revenue strain. They have their work cut out to build up their funding base," he said.
